One more thing worth knowing: in modern Korean, ㅐ and ㅔ are usually pronounced very similarly, so don't stress too much about keeping them perfectly distinct when speaking.
My teacher said batchim can make any of its consonant sounds. Is that correct?

Your teacher is pointing at something real, but the full picture is a bit different. Many consonants can appear in the batchim position in writing, but in spoken Korean they reduce to just 7 distinct sounds. So ㄱ, ㅋ, and ㄲ are all written differently, but when any of them lands at the bottom of a syllable, they all produce the same stopped sound — made without a burst of air. What's written and what's pronounced aren't always the same thing in Korean.
I read that ㅘ sounds like 'ya' — is that right?

You're close on the shape of it, but that's actually ㅑ. ㅘ sounds approximately like 'wa.' It's a compound vowel represented by ㅗ + ㅏ and pronounced approximately 'wa.' The 'ya' family of vowels — ㅑ, ㅕ, ㅛ, ㅠ — all have that 'y' glide at the front, while the 'w' family — ㅘ, ㅝ — start with a 'w' glide instead.
Someone told me ㄲ is just a stronger version of ㄱ with more air. Is that right?

Almost — but the direction is actually reversed. ㄲ is a tense consonant, which means it's produced with more muscular tension and typically less air than the plain ㄱ. The aspirated version — the one with more air — is ㅋ. A useful approximation for ㄲ is the 'k' in 'ski': clipped and tense, without the burst of air you'd hear in 'key'. That said, tense consonants are genuinely tricky to describe in English terms — hearing native examples helps more than any description.
I thought ㅐ and ㅔ sound completely different. They must be easy to tell apart when listening, right?

This one is interesting — historically they were distinct, and some speakers still produce them differently. But for most modern Korean speakers, especially in Seoul, ㅐ and ㅔ are pronounced very similarly, sometimes identically. So if you're having trouble telling them apart by ear, that's not a failure on your part — the distinction has largely merged in everyday speech. Where it still matters is spelling: you'll need to learn which words use which vowel, since the written forms haven't merged even if the sounds often have.
I think ㄱ as batchim sounds like a soft 'g' at the end of a syllable. Is that right?

Your tongue moves into the position for ㄱ, with the back of your tongue contacting the soft palate, but the stop isn't released with a burst of air. Think of the 'k' at the very end of 'back' when you trail off — the position is there but the release isn't. That quality is what makes Korean batchim sound distinct from English final consonants.
Can Korean syllables start with a vowel sound, or do they always need a consonant?

Korean syllable blocks always have something written in the initial position, but when the syllable begins with a vowel sound, the letter ㅇ fills that slot. In initial position, ㅇ has no consonant sound of its own — it's essentially a placeholder that signals 'this syllable starts with the vowel directly.' So 아 is pronounced 'a', not 'nga'. This is different from ㅇ in batchim position, where it does produce a nasal sound, like the 'ng' in 'sing'.

I thought Hangul has 24 letters total — 14 consonants and 10 vowels. Is that right?

I thought a syllable block in Korean is just the letters written in a row, like how English works. Is that right?

Not quite — Korean syllable blocks are arranged spatially rather than linearly. Each block arranges its components within a compact square-like space: the initial consonant, the vowel, and the optional batchim are all positioned relative to each other, not just placed side by side. So 한 isn't ㅎ + ㅏ + ㄴ written in a row — it's those three elements arranged into a single compact unit. That's part of what gives Korean text its distinctive block-like appearance.

English words can give you a rough intuition, but neither 'r' nor 'l' is a reliable guide to how ㄹ actually sounds in Korean — hearing native examples will get you further than any written description.
I thought ㄱ and ㅋ are basically the same sound, just spelled differently. Are they interchangeable?

In Korean the distinction matters — swapping one for the other produces a different word. English approximations can give you a rough intuition for the contrast, but Korean ㄱ and ㅋ each have their own character, and the aspiration difference is what to listen for.

When it appears at the bottom of a block as batchim, it produces a nasal sound, like the 'ng' at the end of 'sing'. So 아 is just 'a', but 강 ends with that nasal sound. The same written letter has different functions depending on its position in the block.

A better approach is to treat it as its own unit — approximately 'wo' in romanization — keeping in mind that's a label rather than an exact English equivalent.

That same pattern holds across Korean — every syllable block needs at minimum an initial consonant and a vowel, and 가 is about as clean an example of that as you'll find.
Are ㄲ, ㄸ, ㅃ, ㅆ, and ㅉ the five tense consonants in Korean?

Unlike aspirated consonants such as ㅋ, ㅌ, ㅍ, and ㅊ, tense consonants aren't produced with a strong burst of air — they're produced with increased muscular tension instead.

If ㅐ and ㅔ sound the same in modern Korean, why do they still have different spellings?

Because the spelling distinction was established when ㅐ and ㅔ represented different sounds, and the written forms have remained distinct even though their pronunciation has largely merged for most modern speakers. Korean spelling preserves that earlier distinction rather than updating to reflect current speech. The practical consequence is that you'll need to learn which vowel belongs in which word through reading and vocabulary practice, rather than working it out from sound alone.
What's the difference between ㄱ, ㅋ, and ㄲ? They all seem like 'k' sounds to me.

They're all in the same consonant family but each has a distinct quality. ㄱ is the plain consonant — no extra tension, no burst of air. ㅋ is aspirated, meaning it comes with a noticeably strong burst of air. ㄲ is tense, produced with increased muscular tension and relatively little air. The easiest contrast to notice at first is often ㅋ against the other two, because the burst of air is the most physically obvious difference. English approximations can give you a rough intuition, but none maps exactly — the important thing is that 가, 카, and 까 are three distinct syllables in Korean, and the difference matters.
How do ㅏ, ㅓ, ㅗ, and ㅜ relate to each other? Are they connected somehow?

They form a natural group — four important Korean vowels that can be compared by tongue position and lip shape. ㅏ is relatively open and unrounded, produced with the mouth fairly wide. ㅓ is more central and also unrounded. ㅗ and ㅜ are both rounded vowels — lips pushed forward — with ㅜ produced with the tongue positioned higher than ㅗ. One way to feel the differences is to say them in sequence and notice how your tongue and lips shift. English words can give you rough listening cues, but none is an exact equivalent, and relying too heavily on English comparisons can mislead you on the finer distinctions.
Why does ㄹ sound different in 라 versus 달? Is it the same letter doing two different things?

Yes — it's the same Hangul consonant, but its pronunciation changes depending on where it appears and what sounds surround it. In 라, ㄹ is in the initial position and tends to have a quick, light quality. In 달, ㄹ is in batchim position and has more of an 'l'-like quality. These feel quite different to ears trained on English, but in Korean they're the same letter behaving differently depending on where it appears. Position in the syllable block is the main driver of which quality you hear.

Try this: bring the back of your tongue up into position for the final consonant, but stop there without releasing a burst. The difference between a pushed-out final consonant and a held one is subtle but real, and it's part of what gives Korean its characteristic sound at the ends of syllables.
I've seen Korean romanized so many different ways — 이 as 'i', 'ee', or 'yi' for example. Is one of them correct and the others wrong?

It depends on which romanization system you're using — romanization is primarily a way of representing Korean in the Latin alphabet, not a one-to-one guide to pronunciation, so different systems make different choices. The current official standard for South Korean Korean is Revised Romanization of Korean, which uses 'i' for ㅣ. Older systems like McCune-Reischauer used different conventions, and informal romanization varies widely. For this app, Revised Romanization is the anchor — but recognizing that other systems exist helps make sense of the variation you'll encounter in textbooks, signage, and online resources.
